plan.contextChunk: This figure contains four panels, (a) through (d), that illustrate the trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair geometry and identify the energetically preferred arrangement of lone pairs in ClF3. Panel (a) shows an unlabeled trigonal bipyramidal frame with arrows identifying the two types of positions: the "Axial" positions at the top and bottom of a vertical axis, and the "Equatorial" positions arranged in a triangular plane around the middle. Panels (b), (c), and (d) each show a Cl atom at the center of the trigonal bipyramidal geometry with three F atoms (labeled F) and two lone pairs (shown as short red bond lines) distributed among the five positions in three distinct arrangements: panel (b) places both lone pairs in equatorial positions, producing the T-shaped molecular structure that is actually observed; panel (c) places one lone pair axial and one equatorial; and panel (d) places both lone pairs in axial positions, the arrangement with the greatest lone-pair–bond-pair repulsion. This figure establishes that lone pairs preferentially occupy the more spacious equatorial positions — where 120° bond angles reduce repulsion — and that this preference uniquely determines the experimentally observed T-shaped geometry of ClF3 within VSEPR theory.

elements: Trigonal bipyramidal wireframe: two apical vertices on a vertical axis plus three equatorial vertices on a horizontal triangle, all connected by olive-green edges
Translucent light-green shaded equatorial triangle (plane through the three equatorial vertices), with its rear edge drawn as a dashed green line
Gray interior bond lines from the central position to the vertices (used where a position holds a normal bond or is unoccupied)
Red short bond lines from the center to the vertices representing lone pairs
Central atom label 'Cl' at the origin of each panel-(b/c/d) structure
Peripheral atom labels 'F' placed just outside the occupied vertices
Panel (a) black leader lines with elbow: vertical line labelled 'Equatorial' pointing to the left equatorial vertex, horizontal line labelled 'Axial' pointing to the top axial vertex
Vertical dashed black separator lines between panels
Panel captions '(a)', '(b)', '(c)', '(d)' centered below each panel
In panels (b)-(d): a left structure (electron-pair geometry with red lone pairs) and a right structure (same frame relabelled with F atoms showing the resulting molecular shape)

interactions.teaches: The trigonal bipyramid is two distinct position sets: three equatorial vertices spread 120° apart in one plane, two axial vertices 90° above and below that plane — a difference invisible in a single flat drawing.

Clicking the 'Axial' or 'Equatorial' label in panel (a) highlights that position set in every panel at once, so the learner can read any arrangement as 'which type of site does each lone pair occupy'.

options: (b) both lone pairs equatorial — observed T-shape
interactions.teaches: Cycling the three candidate ClF3 arrangements shows that only the placement of the two lone pairs changes, and that each placement yields a different molecular shape (T-shaped, trigonal-planar-like, or bent-axial).

interactions.label: Show 90° lone-pair–bond-pair repulsions
interactions.teaches: Counting the 90° lone-pair–bond-pair contacts (4 for panel b, 6 for panel c, 5 for panel d) explains quantitatively why equatorial lone pairs are preferred and why panel (b) is the real geometry of ClF3.

demo_steps.title: Two kinds of positions
demo_steps.narration: The trigonal bipyramid offers two axial sites on the vertical axis and three equatorial sites in the shaded horizontal plane. Orbit the frame: equatorial neighbours sit 120° apart, axial-to-equatorial angles are only 90°.

demo_steps.title: (b) Both lone pairs equatorial
demo_steps.narration: Placing both lone pairs (red) in the roomy equatorial plane leaves F atoms at the two axial sites and one equatorial site — the T-shaped structure actually observed for ClF3.

state.panel: (b) both lone pairs equatorial — observed T-shape

demo_steps.title: (c) Both lone pairs axial
demo_steps.narration: Forcing both lone pairs onto the axis puts each of them 90° from all three bonding pairs — six close lone-pair–bond-pair contacts, the most repulsive option.

demo_steps.title: (d) One axial, one equatorial
demo_steps.narration: A mixed arrangement gives five 90° lone-pair–bond-pair contacts — better than (c) but still worse than (b).

demo_steps.title: Why T-shaped wins
demo_steps.narration: Return to (b) and click the 'Equatorial' label: lone pairs always seek the equatorial sites where 120° separation minimises repulsion, which uniquely fixes the T-shaped geometry of ClF3.

state.panel: (b) both lone pairs equatorial — observed T-shape

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: One trigonal bipyramid: central atom at origin; axial vertices at (0, +1.7, 0) and (0, -1.7, 0); three equatorial vertices at radius 1.35 in the y=0 plane, oriented as in the source so that one points toward the viewer-and-down on screen (azimuth -90°, i.e. +Z toward viewer) and the other two recede left-back and right-back (azimuth 150° and 30°). The rear edge joining the two back equatorial vertices is DASHED; the two front edges are solid. Equatorial triangle filled translucent light green (#DCE9B8, ~45% opacity) with olive-green outline #8CC63F / #7FAF37 (line width ~2.5). Interior bonds from center to vertices are gray #9A9A9A; lone-pair bonds are dark red #A0342A and drawn slightly SHORTER (~70% of the full radius) than the gray bonds. Labels black, sans-serif, ~0.35 units tall. Panels (b)-(d) each contain TWO bipyramids side by side, centers 4.2 units apart in X; the left one carries the 'Cl' label plus red lone-pair lines, the right one carries 'Cl' at center and 'F' labels outside its three occupied vertices. Panel (a) is a single unlabelled frame with black leader lines: a vertical black line from above-left bending horizontally into the LEFT-BACK equatorial vertex, labelled 'Equatorial' at its top; a short horizontal black line entering the TOP AXIAL vertex from the right, labelled 'Axial'. Vertical black dashed separators between panels; caption '(a)'…'(d)' about 2.6 units below each panel center. Arrangement per source image: (b) lone pairs on the right-back and front equatorial vertices → F at top axial, bottom axial, left-back equatorial (T-shaped); (c) lone pairs on BOTH axial vertices (red line running top vertex through center to bottom vertex) → F on all three equatorial vertices; (d) lone pairs on the top axial vertex and the right-back equatorial vertex → F at left-back equatorial, front equatorial, bottom axial. Angles for the repulsion overlay: axial–equatorial = 90°, equatorial–equatorial = 120°, axial–axial = 180°; 90° LP–BP counts are 4 (b), 6 (c), 5 (d).
interactionPlan.notes: Build each bipyramid as a reusable Group: LineSegments (or thick Line2) for the 10 outer edges with the single rear equatorial edge as a LineDashedMaterial (call computeLineDistances), a ShapeGeometry/MeshBasicMaterial triangle with transparent:true, depthWrite:false, side:DoubleSide for the shaded equatorial plane, and per-vertex bond cylinders/lines whose material swaps between gray and red based on the current panel state. Labels (Cl, F, Equatorial, Axial, panel captions) as CSS2DObject or sprite text so they stay screen-facing and legible while orbiting. Panel switching should crossfade or just rebuild bond colors on the same shared frame so the learner sees only the lone pairs move. Highlight mode from the click interaction: emissive/thicker outline plus a soft colored halo on the two axial or three equatorial vertices in every visible structure simultaneously. Repulsion overlay: thin translucent arcs (TorusGeometry segments or line arcs) between each lone pair and each 90°-adjacent bond, with a count badge. Default camera is a standard isometric pose, slight tilt above the equatorial plane so the plane reads as an ellipse; orbit limited in polar angle to keep the vertical axis upright. Flat white background, no shadows, no specular — match the line-art look of the textbook.

authoredContext:
According to VSEPR theory, the terminal atom locations (Xs in ) are equivalent within the linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral electron-pair geometries (the first three rows of the table). It does not matter which X is replaced with a lone pair because the molecules can be rotated to convert positions. For trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair geometries, however, there are two distinct X positions, as shown in : an axial position (if we hold a model of a trigonal bipyramid by the two axial positions, we have an axis around which we can rotate the model) and an equatorial position (three positions form an equator around the middle of the molecule). As shown in , the axial position is surrounded by bond angles of 90°, whereas the equatorial position has more space available because of the 120° bond angles. In a trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair geometry, lone pairs always occupy equatorial positions because these more spacious positions can more easily accommodate the larger lone pairs.

Theoretically, we can come up with three possible arrangements for the three bonds and two lone pairs for the ClF 3 molecule ( ). The stable structure is the one that puts the lone pairs in equatorial locations, giving a T-shaped molecular structure.

(a) In a trigonal bipyramid, the two axial positions are located directly across from one another, whereas the three equatorial positions are located in a triangular arrangement. (b–d) The two lone pairs (red lines) in ClF 3 have several possible arrangements, but the T-shaped molecular structure (b) is the one actually observed, consistent with the larger lone pairs both occupying equatorial positions.

Four sets of images are shown and labeled, “a,” “b,” “c,” and “d.” Each image is separated by a dashed vertical line. Image a shows a six-faced, bi-pyramidal structure where the central vertical axis is labeled, “Axial,” and the horizontal plane is labeled, “Equatorial.” Image b shows a pair of diagrams in the same shape as image a, but in these diagrams, the left has a chlorine atom in the center while the right has a chlorine atom in the center, two fluorine atoms on the upper and lower ends, and one fluorine in the left horizontal position. Image c shows a pair of diagrams in the same shape as image a, but in these diagrams, the left has a chlorine atom in the center while the right has a chlorine atom in the center and three fluorine atoms in each horizontal position. Image d shows a pair of diagrams in the same shape as image a, but in these diagrams, the left has a chlorine atom in the center while the right has a chlorine atom in the center, two fluorine atoms in the horizontal positions, and one in the axial bottom position.

When a central atom has two lone electron pairs and four bonding regions, we have an octahedral electron-pair geometry. The two lone pairs are on opposite sides of the octahedron (180° apart), giving a square planar molecular structure that minimizes lone pair-lone pair repulsions ( ).

discrepancies: The dashed black panel separators in panel (a) are placed at ±3.0 world units, so they cut straight through the 'Equatorial' and 'Axial' text labels, creating clutter that does not exist in the source where separators sit well clear of annotations.

The leader lines in panel (a) are straight single segments; the source uses an L-shaped (vertical + horizontal) leader for 'Equatorial' anchored at the far upper-left, so the annotation geometry reads differently.

The model occupies only a small fraction of the canvas (large empty margins), whereas the source fills its panel — the bipyramid is rendered noticeably smaller than the surrounding annotation/separator extent.

Panel (a) in the source shows all five central gray bonds clearly reaching each vertex; in the render the interior gray bonds are faint/thin and hard to distinguish from the green edges at this scale.
evaluation.notes: A chemically correct, well-structured trigonal-bipyramidal ClF3 figure with faithful colors and a rich, pedagogically meaningful set of interactions (panel tabs, 90° repulsion overlay, axial/equatorial highlighting, guided tour); weaknesses are cosmetic — the model is rendered small in the frame and the dashed panel separators collide with the panel-(a) annotation labels.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are purely cosmetic execution details (separator placement colliding with labels, leader-line shape, model scale, bond thickness) that the generator can fix directly.

interactionPlan.notes: Build each bipyramid as a reusable Group: LineSegments (or thick Line2) for the 10 outer edges with the single rear equatorial edge as a LineDashedMaterial (call computeLineDistances), a ShapeGeometry/MeshBasicMaterial triangle with transparent:true, depthWrite:false, side:DoubleSide for the shaded equatorial plane, and per-vertex bond cylinders/lines whose material swaps between gray and red based on the current panel state. Labels (Cl, F, Equatorial, Axial, panel captions) as CSS2DObject or sprite text so they stay screen-facing and legible while orbiting. Panel switching should crossfade or just rebuild bond colors on the same shared frame so the learner sees only the lone pairs move. Highlight mode from the click interaction: emissive/thicker outline plus a soft colored halo on the two axial or three equatorial vertices in every visible structure simultaneously. Repulsion overlay: thin translucent arcs (TorusGeometry segments or line arcs) between each lone pair and each 90°-adjacent bond, with a count badge. Default camera is a standard isometric pose, slight tilt above the equatorial plane so the plane reads as an ellipse; orbit limited in polar angle to keep the vertical axis upright. Flat white background, no shadows, no specular — match the line-art look of the textbook.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure contains four panels, (a) through (d), that illustrate the trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair geometry and identify the energetically preferred arrangement of lone pairs in ClF3. Panel (a) shows an unlabeled trigonal bipyramidal frame with arrows identifying the two types of positions: the "Axial" positions at the top and bottom of a vertical axis, and the "Equatorial" positions arranged in a triangular plane around the middle. Panels (b), (c), and (d) each show a Cl atom at the center of the trigonal bipyramidal geometry with three F atoms (labeled F) and two lone pairs (shown as short red bond lines) distributed among the five positions in three distinct arrangements: panel (b) places both lone pairs in equatorial positions, producing the T-shaped molecular structure that is actually observed; panel (c) places one lone pair axial and one equatorial; and panel (d) places both lone pairs in axial positions, the arrangement with the greatest lone-pair–bond-pair repulsion. This figure establishes that lone pairs preferentially occupy the more spacious equatorial positions — where 120° bond angles reduce repulsion — and that this preference uniquely determines the experimentally observed T-shaped geometry of ClF3 within VSEPR theory.

discrepancies: Degenerate azimuth: the front equatorial vertex projects exactly onto the vertical axis, so the front edges (apex–EQF) sit on top of the axial bond line — the trigonal bipyramid reads as a flat kite and the axial gray bond is completely hidden, unlike the source where all three equatorial vertices and the internal gray sticks are separately visible.

In panel (a) the source shows five gray internal bonds radiating from the centre to every vertex; in the render only the two rear equatorial gray sticks are visible (axial and front bonds are occluded by the coincident green edges), weakening the 'axial vs equatorial' teaching point.

Camera elevation is higher than the source (≈35° vs ≈20°): the top apex is strongly foreshortened while the bottom apex extends far below, so the bipyramid looks asymmetric instead of the balanced double-pyramid of the original.
Dashed black separator bars are drawn on BOTH sides of the single visible panel; in the source they only sit between adjacent panels, so the current framing reads as an oddly boxed-in single figure.

The source presents all four panels side by side for direct comparison; the generated version shows only one at a time (mitigated by the panel toggle buttons, but the at-a-glance comparative composition is lost).
evaluation.notes: Chemistry (lone-pair placements and 90° repulsion counts for ClF3) is accurate and the interaction set — panel toggles, repulsion arcs, position highlighting and a 5-step guided tour — is rich and pedagogically strong, but the default camera lands on a degenerate azimuth/elevation that collapses the front equatorial vertex onto the vertical axis, hiding the gray axial bond and flattening the bipyramid's 3D read.
action_items: Rotate the default azimuth (e.g. set equatorial vertices at 90°/210°/330° or use az≈30°) so the front equatorial vertex no longer projects onto the vertical axis and the gray axial bond stays visible.
Lower the default elevation to ≈20° so the top and bottom apexes are symmetric about the equatorial rhombus, matching the source's proportions.
Render the internal Cl–X sticks slightly in front (polygonOffset or a small radial inset) so all five gray bonds read clearly in panel (a) as in the source.
Draw the dashed separators only where the source places them (between panels) or offer an 'all panels' view that lays (a)–(d) out side by side for direct comparison.

elements: Trigonal bipyramidal wireframe: two apical vertices on a vertical axis plus three equatorial vertices on a horizontal triangle, all connected by olive-green edges
Translucent light-green shaded equatorial triangle (plane through the three equatorial vertices), with its rear edge drawn as a dashed green line
Gray interior bond lines from the central position to the vertices (used where a position holds a normal bond or is unoccupied)
Red short bond lines from the center to the vertices representing lone pairs
Central atom label 'Cl' at the origin of each panel-(b/c/d) structure
Peripheral atom labels 'F' placed just outside the occupied vertices
Panel (a) black leader lines with elbow: vertical line labelled 'Equatorial' pointing to the left equatorial vertex, horizontal line labelled 'Axial' pointing to the top axial vertex
Vertical dashed black separator lines between panels
Panel captions '(a)', '(b)', '(c)', '(d)' centered below each panel

interactions.teaches: The trigonal bipyramid is two distinct position sets: three equatorial vertices spread 120° apart in one plane, two axial vertices 90° above and below that plane — a difference invisible in a single flat drawing.

Clicking the 'Axial' or 'Equatorial' label in panel (a) highlights that position set in every panel at once, so the learner can read any arrangement as 'which type of site does each lone pair occupy'.

options: (b) both lone pairs equatorial — observed T-shape
interactions.teaches: Cycling the three candidate ClF3 arrangements shows that only the placement of the two lone pairs changes, and that each placement yields a different molecular shape (T-shaped, trigonal-planar-like, or bent-axial).

interactions.label: Show 90° lone-pair–bond-pair repulsions
interactions.teaches: Counting the 90° lone-pair–bond-pair contacts (4 for panel b, 6 for panel c, 5 for panel d) explains quantitatively why equatorial lone pairs are preferred and why panel (b) is the real geometry of ClF3.

demo_steps.title: Two kinds of positions
demo_steps.narration: The trigonal bipyramid offers two axial sites on the vertical axis and three equatorial sites in the shaded horizontal plane. Orbit the frame: equatorial neighbours sit 120° apart, axial-to-equatorial angles are only 90°.

demo_steps.title: (b) Both lone pairs equatorial
demo_steps.narration: Placing both lone pairs (red) in the roomy equatorial plane leaves F atoms at the two axial sites and one equatorial site — the T-shaped structure actually observed for ClF3.

state.panel: (b) both lone pairs equatorial — observed T-shape

demo_steps.title: (c) Both lone pairs axial
demo_steps.narration: Forcing both lone pairs onto the axis puts each of them 90° from all three bonding pairs — six close lone-pair–bond-pair contacts, the most repulsive option.

demo_steps.title: (d) One axial, one equatorial
demo_steps.narration: A mixed arrangement gives five 90° lone-pair–bond-pair contacts — better than (c) but still worse than (b).

demo_steps.title: Why T-shaped wins
demo_steps.narration: Return to (b) and click the 'Equatorial' label: lone pairs always seek the equatorial sites where 120° separation minimises repulsion, which uniquely fixes the T-shaped geometry of ClF3.

state.panel: (b) both lone pairs equatorial — observed T-shape

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: One trigonal bipyramid: central atom at origin; axial vertices at (0, +1.7, 0) and (0, -1.7, 0); three equatorial vertices at radius 1.35 in the y=0 plane, oriented as in the source so that one points toward the viewer-and-down on screen (azimuth -90°, i.e. +Z toward viewer) and the other two recede left-back and right-back (azimuth 150° and 30°). The rear edge joining the two back equatorial vertices is DASHED; the two front edges are solid. Equatorial triangle filled translucent light green (#DCE9B8, ~45% opacity) with olive-green outline #8CC63F / #7FAF37 (line width ~2.5). Interior bonds from center to vertices are gray #9A9A9A; lone-pair bonds are dark red #A0342A and drawn slightly SHORTER (~70% of the full radius) than the gray bonds. Labels black, sans-serif, ~0.35 units tall. Panels (b)-(d) each contain TWO bipyramids side by side, centers 4.2 units apart in X; the left one carries the 'Cl' label plus red lone-pair lines, the right one carries 'Cl' at center and 'F' labels outside its three occupied vertices. Panel (a) is a single unlabelled frame with black leader lines: a vertical black line from above-left bending horizontally into the LEFT-BACK equatorial vertex, labelled 'Equatorial' at its top; a short horizontal black line entering the TOP AXIAL vertex from the right, labelled 'Axial'. Vertical black dashed separators between panels; caption '(a)'…'(d)' about 2.6 units below each panel center. Arrangement per source image: (b) lone pairs on the right-back and front equatorial vertices → F at top axial, bottom axial, left-back equatorial (T-shaped); (c) lone pairs on BOTH axial vertices (red line running top vertex through center to bottom vertex) → F on all three equatorial vertices; (d) lone pairs on the top axial vertex and the right-back equatorial vertex → F at left-back equatorial, front equatorial, bottom axial. Angles for the repulsion overlay: axial–equatorial = 90°, equatorial–equatorial = 120°, axial–axial = 180°; 90° LP–BP counts are 4 (b), 6 (c), 5 (d).
